summary: Former U.S. Forest Service fire tower on the Satulah summit, undated in the sources; summit bought 1909, in a 1995 NRHP district, now a land trust preserve.

facts.status_note: Sources describe a former fire tower; none describes one standing on the summit today.

access.note: The Satulah Mountain Preserve is one of the Highlands-Cashiers Land Trust's nine public properties.

visit.trail_note: Three-mile hike rated difficult and aimed at experienced hikers; the remains of a stone shelter are at the top.

events.note: Highlands townspeople raised $500 and bought 56 acres on Satulah Mountain to keep a hotel off the summit. A local list credits the Highlands Improvement Society with the 1909 summit item.
Satulah Mountain Historic District listed on the National Register of Historic Places; the summit is one of its listed entries.

evidence.supports: A list of North Carolina lookout towers includes Satulah Mtn in Macon County.
Satulah Mountain is located within several miles of downtown Highlands.
evidence.quote: One such is Satulah Mountain, which is located within several miles of downtown Highlands.

evidence.supports: In 1909 members of the town of Highlands raised $500 and bought 56 acres to keep a hotel from the summit.
evidence.quote: It all started in 1909 when members of the town of Highlands banded together and raised $500 to purchase 56 acres on Satulah Mountain in order to save it from the construction of a hotel.

evidence.supports: The goal was to keep the summit in its natural state as a public park.
evidence.quote: The goal was to preserve the summit in its natural state as a public park for the community.

evidence.supports: The 1909 summit item is credited to the Highlands Improvement Society.
evidence.quote: Satulah Mountain Summit (Highlands Improvement Society, 1909), top of mountain (NR)

evidence.supports: A small stone shelter was built for overnight hikers, and the summit later housed a Forest Service fire tower and cottage.
evidence.quote: A small stone shelter was constructed for overnight hikers, later Satulah housed a U.S. Forest Service fire tower and cottage.

evidence.supports: Potholes in the rock are said to be evidence of a fire tower that once stood on the summit.
evidence.quote: The potholes in the rock surface are said to be evidence of a fire tower that once stood on the summit.

evidence.supports: The Satulah Mountain Historic District was added to the National Register on October 5, 1995.
The summit is listed as an entry within the district, which was NR-listed in 1995.
The district is residential, with log houses and Craftsman features.
evidence.quote: is a residential historic district in Highlands, North Carolina

evidence.supports: The Highlands-Cashiers Land Trust has nine public properties, including the Satulah Mountain Preserve.
evidence.quote: The organization has nine properties that are open to the public.

evidence.supports: The Satulah Mountain Preserve has a three-mile hike rated difficult.
The summit today has the remains of the stone shelter and a 270-degree view, and no tower is described.
evidence.quote: Today, the Satulah Mountain Preserve is home to a three-mile hike for experienced hikers with the remains of the stone shelter and a 270-degree vista that overlooks North Carolina, South Carolina and Georgia.

evidence.supports: The district has a number of log houses.
evidence.quote: There are a number of log houses

evidence.supports: Many houses in the district have Craftsman features.
The summit is item 12 in the list's District 1, the Satulah Mountain Historic District.
evidence.quote: District 1: Satulah Mountain Historic District, bounded by Walhalla Rd.

corrections.why: AE5633 has the form of an NGS survey-mark ID rather than a lookout register number. The list's last column shows 'bm' for entries that have no such code. This is an inference from the list, not checked against NGS.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The magazine credits members of the town of Highlands; the historic structures list credits the Highlands Improvement Society. Both may describe one effort, so the story names both sources without choosing.

sources.title: The Highlands-Cashiers Land Trust's public hiking destinations
Satulah has long been a WNC favorite
A List of Historic Structures In and Around Highlands

notes_for_editor: No source dates the fire tower or says when it came down; status 'gone' rests on 'once stood' (cite 3) and the magazine's past-tense wording. The 1909 shelter is undated. The NRHP nomination that Wikipedia cites (NC SHPO) was not fetched and may date the tower and shelter. Access is from the land trust's own list in the magazine article and has not been checked against the land trust's site. The tnlandforms code AE5633 is probably an NGS survey mark, so the NGS register entry is proposed for removal.
